newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Oxford dons row over business school.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oxford dons row over business school.

text.p: Oxford, one of the world's oldest and most prestigious universities, is embroiled in an ungentlemanly row over subjects close to many English hearts -- money, cricket and foreigners.

Some say the conflict is a showdown between elitist academics and capitalism. Others see it as a phoney war that will be resolved without any bloodshed. Many smell hypocrisy in the rarefied air surrounding Oxford's "dreaming spires".
The first skirmish took place on November 5 when Oxford dons (university academics) voted by 259 to 214 to reject using one of its several sporting grounds as the site for a new business school.

Most objected to the destruction of a favourite cricket ground. But outsiders saw the vote as a snub for Wafic Rida Said, a Syrian-born businessman who offered 20 million pounds ($33.67 million) to fund the project.

Said, a friend of former conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher, has been accused of making part of his estimated 200 million pound fortune through arms dealing -- a charge he strenously denies.
John Gray, professor of politics at Oxford, who favours the new business school, blames the "excesses of Thatcherism" for the vote against it.
"The assault of Thatcherism on old institutions in the name of business and promoting the market, although perhaps necessary to start with, became crude ideological doctrine," Gray said.
Thatcher is not well loved by Oxford academics. In 1985 they voted against bestowing an honorary degree on the "Iron Lady".
Gray said many academics rejected the creation of "profit centres" in Britain's national institutions such as the health service or the BBC -- policies put in place under Thatcher.
These dons, safe in their Oxford sinecures, believe playing a good game on the sports field is a more gentlemanly pursuit than creating wealth in the market place, Gray said.
Anthony Smith, the president of Magdalen College, agrees that antagonism towards wealth "tainted" by the profit motive did play a part in the negative vote -- but only a minor part.
"People have the wrong story. This is about a cricket pitch, not business studies or Mr Said's money," Smith said.
Smith believes only around 13 of the 259 dissenters in the November vote opposed taking Said's cash.
Around 85 percent of the academics who voted "no" objected to the use of the much-loved cricket ground which the university had agreed to keep as a green field in perpetuity, he said.
"Perhaps 10 percent had reservations about business studies in general, but that really doesn't matter. Oxford already has a business studies department. We already award business degrees."
Another vote on the issue will take place in February, allowing 3,200 academics, senior library and administrative staff to decide the issue.
Smith expects an overwhelming vote in favour of accepting Said's millions. If necessary, a new site for the business school will be found that is acceptable to all parties involved.

Gray hopes Smith is right but is not convinced. He believes a large number of dons hold a deep hostility to management studies which they consider "faddish" and out of keeping with the classical disciplines of the 800-year-old university.
"It is true that many business books have been jargon-ridden. They invite scepticism by their claim to have found a panacea against economic and business failure," he said.
But Gray said the appointment of Professor John Kay, a highly regarded academic, as director of the business school might silence critics.

"A programme of management studies led by him would put Oxford not only at the forefront of the 100 or more British business schools, but would also be an important step in challenging the American lead in world markets," Gray said.
"No one can question his intellectual credentials. Professor Kay is one of the best economists of his generation." Kay may decline his appointment if the new building is turned down.

Gray said it was "ironic" that some colleagues were reluctant to take money from someone perhaps connected with the arms trade. He noted one of the University's distinguished institutions, Rhodes House, was founded by a colonial adventurer Cecil Rhodes.
"Some of the people who originally founded (Oxford) colleges certainly by our standards and even by the standards of their cultures at the time, sailed close to the wind," Gray said.

Battles between the University and the outside world over money are nothing new. Since the Middle Ages there have been conflicts between Oxford's poor residents and university members, who historians say would sometimes flaunt their riches.
Antagonism reached its climax in Oxford in 1355 with the Massacre of St Scholastica's Day, when townsmen fought until the streets ran with blood.
Oxford streets are not likely to be bloodied this time around but Gray fears the university will be dealt a body blow if his colleagues prefer bats and balls to business.
"Britain stands between the business cultures of Europe and North America. We need an institution which expresses that unique role in Europe," Gray said.
"If it is voted down again we may not see a new business school in Oxford for a very long time."
